html:
Haida Gwaii, "islands of the people", is an archipelago off the north coast of British Columbia and the homeland of the Haida. In 1492 the Haida lived in large cedar-plank villages along its shores, and some later settled in southern Alaska.

They were the great seafarers of the Northwest Coast, travelling far in big dugout canoes made from single cedar trunks, to trade and to raid neighbours such as the Tsimshian, Heiltsuk and Tlingit. Their carved totem poles and the potlatch feasts where chiefs gave away wealth to show their rank are among the best-known arts of the coast.

European traders came from the 1770s for sea otter furs. Then the smallpox epidemic of 1862 and later diseases cut the Haida from perhaps tens of thousands to under a thousand by 1900, and survivors gathered in two villages, Skidegate and Old Massett. The abandoned village of SGang Gwaay, with its standing poles, is a World Heritage Site. The artist Bill Reid helped revive Haida art, and in 2010 Canada officially dropped the name Queen Charlotte Islands.
